catalog_quote: [p.130] Primary stress must normally fall on either the penultimate or the antepenultimate syllable of a syntactic word. There is a strong numerical preference for the penultimate. ... For convenience, I refer to this constraint as the penultimate constraint in the ensuing discussion. [p.131] ... The final syllable of syntactic words is extrametrical (Hayes 1982). ... However any modelling which set up penultimate stress as a basic pattern would have to analyse ante-penultimate stress as resulting from lexically marked exceptions. There is such a quantity of these exceptions that it becomes altogether doubtful whether an analysis which posits penultimate stress as the basic pattern captures any significant generalisation. new_statements.quote: [p.130] Primary stress must normally fall on either the penultimate or the antepenultimate syllable of a syntactic word. There is a strong numerical preference for the penultimate. [...] [p.132] Rhythm does not play a part in the placement of primary stress. Neither does syllable weight, though it may have played a minor role historically (5-41 following). Stress placement in Gaagudju is in large measure an idiosyncratic property of lexical entries, and this is the fundamental aspect in which Gaagudju fails to conform to the tenets underlying metrical theories. [...] The great majority of nominal roots show either penultimate or ante-penultimate stress. Disyllabic nominal roots take stress on the first syllable.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress is lexically specified within a right-edge window: it falls on the penult or the antepenult of the syntactic word (final syllable treated as extrametrical), with penult more frequent (3-syllable nominal roots 166 penult : 42 antepenult; 4-syll 61:53; 5-syll 28:19); which of the two cannot be predicted from rhythm or syllable weight. Disyllabic roots are initial (=penult) stressed. In verbs, stress is lexically listed on simple/compound verb roots and on directional, ergative and tense prefixes (compound verb roots usually stress their last syllable), and repair rules shift these stresses to satisfy the penultimate constraint. Stressed vowels are nearly all long and most long vowels are stressed (4.5.4); the main correlate of primary stress is a sharp pitch rise.
new_statements.secondary_stress: p.130: 'The main auditory correlate of secondary stress is rhythm. As far as I can determine, both disyllabic and trisyllabic rhythmic feet occur (5.6.3). These feet are initial-headed and appear to be erected left-to-right. However, the factors controlling the distribution of the two feet types are unclear.. no analysis of secondary stress is presented in this grammar.'
new_statements.exceptions: A few nominal roots stress outside the (ante)penult window, listed in (5-6), e.g. dja'marrabarday 'brolga', djo'rloorlobarray 'doe kangaroo', gudj'boolombida 'flying fox' (some historically cliticised/derived); a small set of roots with stressed short vowels (4-39) and two with unstressed long vowels (4-37/38); verbal paradigms show morphologically conditioned stress shifts (5.1.2) and one paradigm (5-58) retains traces of an older delimitative initial-stress system (5.1.4).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the 'syntactic word' with final-syllable extrametricality; 'stress' in the grammar means primary stress unless stated; statements are about word-level (citation-form) stress, not phrasal prominence.
new_statements.identity_note: Harvey 1992 describes Gaagudju as spoken by the last fluent speakers in the Kakadu/Oenpelli area (data collected 1980s); no dialect split is distinguished for stress. Same language as gaga1251; the 2002 Mouton grammar is the published revision of this thesis.

sources.note: Primary stress (pitch-rise correlate) must normally fall on the penult or antepenult of the syntactic word (final syllable extrametrical), penult numerically preferred, but the choice is largely a lexical idiosyncrasy; rhythm and syllable weight play no role; disyllabic nominal roots are initial-stressed; verb stress lexically listed on roots/certain prefixes with repair rules enforcing the penultimate constraint; secondary stress rhythmic (left-headed di/trisyllabic feet, L-to-R) but left unanalysed; nearly all stressed vowels long (4.5.4).
